title: Threads, the thread pool and data races
body: A thread is an independent path of execution. `new Thread(Work).Start()` creates a dedicated OS thread, which is expensive; most code instead queues work to the shared thread pool via `Task.Run`, `ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem`, async continuations or `Parallel`. The pool grows and shrinks its threads to balance throughput.

When threads share mutable data without coordination you get a data race. `count++` is a read, an add and a write; two threads can read the same old value and both write old+1, losing an update. The result varies from run to run, which makes races hard to reproduce and test.

`Interlocked` provides atomic operations on single variables: `Increment`, `Add`, `Exchange` and `CompareExchange` (compare-and-swap). They are the cheapest correct fix for counters and flags. For anything involving more than one variable, use a lock (next lesson) or an immutable snapshot swapped in with `Interlocked.Exchange`.

Compilers and CPUs may reorder memory operations as long as single-threaded behaviour is preserved, so one thread may observe another's writes in a surprising order. Locks and `Interlocked` operations include the necessary memory barriers; `Volatile.Read`/`Volatile.Write` give ordering for single fields. Avoid writing lock-free code beyond simple counters unless you have studied the .NET memory model.

The safest shared state is no shared state: give each thread its own data and combine results at the end, or communicate through channels. Before sharing a variable between threads, check every read and write path for atomicity and visibility.

challenge: Start 8 tasks that each add the numbers 1..1000 to a shared long total using Interlocked.Add, wait for all of them and print the total.
question: Why can `count++` from several threads lose updates?
correct: It is a separate read, add and write that other threads can interleave with
wrong: Because ints are 64-bit on modern CPUs
Because the GC moves count between threads
reasoning: Use Interlocked.Increment or a lock so the read-modify-write is atomic.
